$schema_note: User-visible product improvements, newest first. Feeds the pipeline's What's-new card and the homepage footer's latest-improvement stamp — one source, both surfaces (the homepage must match the real site). Keep entries honest, dated, and user-phrased; trim to ~12.

entries.title: The public pages, walked as a visitor on a phone
entries.blurb: Every public page was opened from a production build at phone and desktop widths and read the way a first-time visitor reads it. The covered-markets page ran edge to edge when you were signed out — it now sits in the same measure as the header. Three glued words on the homepage ('aboutabout half a minute', '9real scenarios') came from a compiler quirk that drops a space before a line break when the sentence carries an apostrophe; every such sentence across the app now spells its space. The 'Built in the open' cards clamp a long note to four lines with a link to the full log, and the log itself folds any note longer than a paragraph behind its opening sentences. The sample deal's model slideshow no longer leaves a screen of blank space under the Returns view on a phone. Two tests now stand guard: one scans every page's source for the exact shape the compiler glues, and one renders every section of the deal page on the sample deal and reads the text for a digit run into a word or a word doubled — so the next such sentence fails in CI, not on a visitor's phone. The signed-in screens a visitor never sees — the pipeline, the deal page, the model, the compare table, the assumption bridge, the BOV reconciler, the rent roll, the analytics charts — are now rendered on fixtures in the test suite and opened at phone width in a headless browser too: the pipeline header no longer runs past the viewport at the deal limit, a phone shows each deal's price, cap and fit on their own line instead of behind an ellipsis, the bridge's before and after columns read as dollars and percentages rather than raw model inputs, and the reconciler's copied gap sentence keeps NOI in capitals.

entries.title: Every portfolio view knows the deal's kind — analytics, the meeting export, the shared screen
entries.blurb: The deal page had learned to read a conversion or a development as a plan rather than a stabilized building; three surfaces that add deals up or hand them to someone else had not. Analytics counted a conversion's 11.7% stabilized cap as a going-in cap, so one plan deal could drag the portfolio's median. Now every row is read for its kind first: a plan deal carries its yield on cost and never a cap; the cap tile, the cap chart and the market table say how many plan deals sit outside the cap series and give their median yield on cost; and a plan deal's price per unit is its total cost over the planned units, never the shell's price over apartments that do not exist yet. The pipeline's meeting .xlsx gains a Deal type column and a Yield on cost column beside Cap rate — a conversion's cap cell reads 'n/a — plan' instead of a dash a reader would take for 'not stated', the yield header explains what the figure is, and the summary sheet counts the live plan deals. And the read-only share link a partner or lender opens now names the kind in its subtitle and carries the plan above the key terms — stabilized NOI, price, budget, total cost and yield on cost, the same five facts as the deal page from one source — with one sentence on how to read them, so a $21M stabilized NOI beside a $20M price no longer looks like a misprint. The 'From your pipeline' comp memory on each deal page reads its sibling screens the same way: a conversion you screened earlier is labelled as one, shows its yield on cost where a cap would sit, and its basis is total cost over the planned units, 'all-in', never the shell's price over apartments that do not exist yet. And the since-last-screen diff on a re-screened plan deal tracks the finished project's NOI, the capital budget and the yield on cost as they move, and never mistakes a stabilized cap for the going-in cap. A ground-up development's land cost is its price on all of them. And the readers behind every one of these surfaces read the row they are named for: a 'Unit mix' or 'Unit sizes' row never counts as the building's unit count (so no per-unit figure divides by forty), a 'Sale price', 'List price' or 'Whisper' row is the price (so no sibling drops out of the comp memory or the meeting export), and a re-screen that names the cost two ways — total project cost, then construction budget — is no longer read as a $20M retrade. The same two readers now sit behind every surface that needs them — the market and comp memories, the plausibility check, the Excel model's unit count, the pipeline row, the deal page's summary and the debt sizer — so a 'Vacant units' row is never the building's count, a 'Last sale price' is never the ask, and a development's land cost is its price on the pipeline and the deal page too. The count reader takes every name an OM gives the whole count — total apartment units, number of units, keys, rooms, beds, pads, storage units — while a partial count ('Units under renovation') never passes; 'Pricing' is the price and a reserve or bid figure is not; and a rent per unit never passes a basis ceiling as the price per unit. The building's size is read the same way — 'Total SF', 'Rentable SF', 'GBA', never a land, unit or component figure — so a size check and a $/SF basis are never taken over the lot. And the Excel model's 'In-Place Occupancy' is today's figure, never the sponsor's stabilized one. A third review closed eight more: 'Asking Rent' and 'Price / Key' are never the price, and '250,000 Sq. Ft.' is a building size again. A fourth closed twelve: an occupancy cost or growth is never the occupancy and a row with no percentage never shadows it, a value naming two square footages is neither, a bare 'Size' beside a stated lot is the land's only when the two figures agree, an 'Exit price' or a 'Sale price (2019)' is never the ask, a land cost beside a WALT or a T-12 is an operating asset, and the first signal's ask fills a price slot only when it is a figure — never an 'Unpriced' printed where a price goes. A fifth, on the whole reader code rather than a diff, closed sixteen: an 'Opex per unit' row never clears a basis dealbreaker the price per unit trips, a 'Price per home' or a 'Projected sale price (Year 5)' is never the ask, a Year-3 cap is never the going-in cap, an occupancy whose value says stabilized is not today's, a deck that names its construction budget and proposed units but no strategy is read as a development so its land cost is its price, and the buy box's price band and the mandate's ceiling judge that land cost through the one price reader every surface prints. Nothing changes on a stabilized asset. A sixth closed twelve more: an 'Avg SF / unit' or 'Beds per unit' row is never the price per unit, so a basis ceiling and a hard dealbreaker no longer clear at $912/unit beside a $252k/unit price; a Year-1 NOI is today's income, so a newly built asset listing its construction cost stays an operating asset instead of flipping to a development with an $80M total cost; a Year-3, Year-10 or 2028 cap is never the going-in cap and 'Capitalization rate' reads; 'Size (SF): 250,000' is a building size again; the plausibility check reads the cap through the same reader as every other surface, so a residual or on-cost cap manufactures no finding; an ask dated this year reads while a past year is a prior trade; '94% (Target: 95%)' reads 94; an unpriced ask row yields to a development's land cost; and the compare page, the pipeline export and the analysis-ready email judge the buy box on the same inferred kind as the deal page. A seventh, on the layer that turns those readings into figures, closed twelve more: the public sample report now runs the sample's rent roll and T-12 exactly as the page beside it does, so its grids and its max bid are the page's; '$18,000 per unit' is a rate, never an $18k budget; a development's construction budget is no longer thrown away because its land is a tenth of the works; a total project cost stated beside no asking price reaches the workbook; a development's land price is never held to an apartment market's per-unit band as a misread; the market memory, the analytics price-per-unit series and the pipeline row read a plan deal the way every other surface already did; the workbook leaves out per-square-foot yardsticks over an assumed building size and says why; the model's yield on cost carries the dark years' cost the IRR already spent; and an OM's in-place occupancy sets the vacancy line instead of a class default printed beside it.

entries.title: A plan deal is judged on yield on cost — now stressed, on the deal page
entries.blurb: A conversion, development, lease-up or value-add is built for the spread between what the finished project yields on everything it cost and the cap rate that product trades at once it is done — not for a cap rate against the price. Under the plan strip, every plan deal now carries a 5×5 grid: stabilized NOI 10–20% under the pro forma down the rows, budget 10–30% over the OM's across, each cell the yield on total cost and its spread over the model's own exit cap in basis points, coloured by development-spread band (200+ bps, 150–199, 75–149, under 75, below the cap). Two exact sentences sit under it: how far the stabilized NOI can miss before the spread is gone, and how big an overrun takes the yield down to the cap. A pro forma that keeps its spread in the worst corner is conservative; one that needs its own base case is not — which is the question the challenger is asked. The full report carries the same page — the plan as the OM states it, the grid, the two sentences — ahead of the IRR grids, which an operating-asset model cannot fill for a building that is dark for two years. When the OM's budget appears only in its own words rather than as a line item, it is read from there. And the debt story follows the plan: the Financing & capital card sizes a construction or bridge loan to total cost with the interest reserve inside it, tests the take-out the finished NOI can carry at stabilization, names the cash-in refinance when the two disagree, and shows yield on cost with the carry included. In the pipeline, a plan deal's row shows that yield on cost, labelled, where a stabilized asset shows its cap. The Excel workbook names the deal type on its cover, summary and assumptions tabs, and its budget line carries the OM page it came from; a linked submarket's supply warning tells a plan deal it delivers into that pipeline; ask-the-deal, the 30-second first signal, the broker-comp scrutiny, the market check and the model reconciler are told what kind of deal it is — a conversion's sale comps are held against total cost per finished unit, never the shell's price, and its rent comps against the rents behind the stabilized pro forma — so a yield on cost or a pro forma cap is never quoted as the price's cap; the buy-box check, the mandate score, the market memory, the compare table and the leverage check all read one going-in cap that excludes the finished project's figure — a conversion no longer clears a mandate floor on its stabilized cap; and a ground-up development's price is its land or site cost when the OM states no asking price, never an appraised land value. An OM that states an all-in total cost and no price at all — a sponsor who already owns the land — still states a total cost: the plan strip, the stressed grid, the construction sizer and the report all read it as the total, the yield on cost computes, and nothing calls the figure 'less the price'. And the extraction is now asked for the plan's rows by name — total project cost, construction or renovation budget, land cost on a development, proposed units, construction period, lease-up period, stabilized-in — so the next screen of a plan deal fills the strip from the OM's own lines — and for the headline rows too: Asking price, Units, Total SF, Occupancy and Going-in cap rate, each with the number alone in the value and its look-alikes (a price per unit, a vacant-unit count, a land area, a stabilized occupancy or cap) under their own labels, so every surface lands on the same row. The LOI draft follows the plan too: a conversion or a development carries an entitlements contingency — the approvals a change of use or a ground-up build closes on — and every plan deal's diligence clause names the structural, environmental, zoning and construction-cost work, with the clauses renumbered around it. The property-actuals check reads the kind too: on a plan deal the uploaded T-12 is held against the OM's in-place figure, the stabilized pro forma is never compared to today's actuals, and when the OM states only the finished project's NOI the card and the challenger both say there is nothing to compare — and ask for the in-place figure. Nothing is invented: no stated budget or stabilized NOI, no grid and no loan.

entries.title: News is never empty: live headlines from the publishers, ranked, linked
entries.blurb: The News page waited on a weekday sweep that had not yet run, so it sat empty. It now opens with the day's real estate headlines read live from the publishers' own feeds — Commercial Observer, The Real Deal, GlobeSt, Multi-Housing News, Commercial Property Executive, Connect CRE, REBusinessOnline and the Federal Reserve — plus Google News topic searches on commercial real estate, multifamily, CRE debt and rent regulation, each naming its outlet. Headlines are ranked by recency and by how much they touch what moves a deal (rates, cap rates, distress, regulation, supply), refreshed every half hour, every one linking straight to the article. The sources that answered are listed under the headlines; any that did not are named rather than papered over. The scored, buyer-specific feed still follows once the sweep runs.

entries.title: The deal's strategy is read first — a conversion no longer screens as a stabilized building
entries.blurb: An office-to-residential conversion came through with a Year-1 NOI above its asking price: a 105% cap rate, shown as fact. The OM's $21M was the finished building's stabilized pro forma, years and a construction budget away, and the screen had read it as today's income. Every deal now carries a strategy — stabilized, value-add, lease-up, conversion or development — read from the OM and shown in the header, and every NOI is labelled as in-place, Year 1 or stabilized pro forma. On a deal with a plan, the header shows the plan as the OM states it — stabilized NOI, price, budget, total cost and yield on cost — and the challenger is asked to test whether that stabilized figure is as conservative as the deck says; it is never called a misread. On a deal read as stabilized, an NOI at or above a quarter of the price, a stated cap that disagrees with NOI ÷ price, or a per-unit basis no market trades at is named on the page, put to the challenger and carried into the verdict. The Excel model anchors year 1 on today's income and books the construction budget, and a generated model that treats the finished building's NOI as year 1 says so above its returns. A building's history is not a plan: an OM's 'year built / renovated' row or a 'newly renovated' note never turns a stabilized asset into a value-add — only a renovation program, budget or plan does. The Sep 8 entry carries the follow-through: the stressed yield on cost, the report, the debt story and every surface that reads a cap.

entries.title: Building photos and maps now point at the building
entries.blurb: For most deals the picture was of the wrong place. The geocoder put a street address on the street's centreline or on the city, the app called that point 'the building', and the aerial, the Street View photo and the map pin all inherited the error. Street addresses now go to the US Census Bureau's geocoder first, which matches the house number to the right block face; how precisely a point was found — building, block or area — is read off the answer, and every frame, pin label and photo attempt is honest about it. The Street View camera is aimed at the building rather than at the spot it was standing on, and the USGS aerial resolves one zoom level sharper. Existing deals re-place themselves on their next view.

entries.title: Submarkets live on Market data now
entries.blurb: Submarkets never needed a section of their own — a submarket is part of the market picture. The list and the create form now sit on Market data as 'Your submarkets', next to your own comp memory. Each submarket's own page, the deal-page assumption check and every old link still work; /submarkets simply lands on the panel.

entries.title: Verification sweep — every internal link checked, and a scope contradiction caught
entries.blurb: A full crawl of the public site: all 41 pages (every metro brief, all 14 sector tabs, every marketing page) return 200, and all 53 unique internal links resolve — no dead ends. The sweep also caught the homepage contradicting itself: the pulse board counted its 18 jurisdiction tiles as though each were a market, while the same page said '15 markets, deliberately.' DC, Prince George's, Montgomery and Northern Virginia are four tiles inside one DMV-core market, so the board now reads '18 jurisdiction tiles across 15 covered markets,' both numbers derived. Three tests pin the counts so a future market can't reopen the gap.

entries.title: Which assumption moved the IRR — the assumption bridge
entries.blurb: Re-run a deal with a lower price and a tighter exit cap and the return jumps, but nothing used to say which change did the work. It can't be answered one-at-a-time either: cutting price is worth more after the cap tightens than before it, so the answer depends on the order. The bridge uses Shapley values over the changed assumptions instead — order-independent, exact to six changed fields and sampled above that, with the waterfall's bars summing to the headline move exactly. Every model run is snapshotted as a version, so the comparison is always available.

entries.title: Two brokers, one asset — the BOV reconciler
entries.blurb: JLL says $71.5M, Eastdil says $65M, and finding where the $6.5M lives used to take an afternoon in Excel. Upload both and the gap decomposes into Year-1 NOI, cap rate and capex treatment, using the symmetric split so the answer doesn't depend on which factor you apply first. Anything the identity can't explain is shown as unexplained rather than smoothed away, a cap rate backed out of a value and an NOI is labelled derived rather than stated, and each broker's price then runs through your own model so you see the levered IRR each one actually implies.

entries.title: Rent rolls in, and an Excel model whose formulas are alive
entries.blurb: Broker rent rolls are never the same twice — the header is rarely row 1, the columns never match, and rent is monthly on one file and annual on the next. Upload a CSV or XLSX, correct whatever the column mapper missed (it remembers, so the next file from the same broker is one click), and get WALT weighted by both SF and rent, the rollover schedule, mark-to-market and the rollover cost forecast. Then download a four-tab workbook that is a real model: change the exit cap on the Assumptions tab and the IRR recalculates. CI proves it, recalculating the generated file in LibreOffice and asserting its IRR matches the app's to four decimals.

entries.title: Exit cap and rent growth, checked against the submarket
entries.blurb: The two assumptions that swing returns most are usually just typed in, and nothing checks them — a deal underwritten to 4% rent growth in a market with 18 months of supply under construction is a bad deal that screens well. Build a submarket from your own market export and those assumptions get measured against what it actually did: months of supply, trailing rent CAGR on a consistent basis, trough vacancy. Four data traps are handled by name — data-center campuses excluded by a persistent rule, rent-basis changes breaking the trend line instead of being averaged through, a pipeline that doesn't tie reconciled with the delta shown, and round-number placeholders flagged for review. Overriding a warning is normal; it needs a one-line reason, and the reason lands in the memo.

entries.title: The whole board — every market and asset class in one grid
entries.blurb: The market page gains a coverage grid: 18 metro entries down, office/industrial/multifamily/retail across, each cell that market's vacancy read. Shading is computed within each column, so office compares to office — DC industrial at 7.4% shades tight while DC retail at 6.3% shades loose, because those are different worlds. 66 of the 72 cells carry a sourced figure; the other 6 render as dashed gaps that say why rather than implying coverage that isn't there. Bands stay bands throughout.

entries.title: Deal pages: benchmark units follow the metric, and vacancy rows get pack positions
entries.blurb: The vs-market panel on deal pages printed every benchmark with a dollar sign — including percent figures, so an office deal read 'office vacancy: $17.7–$22.3'. Units now follow the metric: vacancy, cap rates, and the 30-yr PMMS print as percents, rents as $/SF, sales and listing counts plain, medians and FMRs keep their dollars — locked in by unit tests. And each vacancy row now carries the metro's rank across the covered markets, from the same shared builder as the rankings, the briefs, and the sample screen — the deal page is the fourth surface that can never disagree.

entries.title: The changelog becomes a tour — every improvement links to where it landed
entries.blurb: What's-new now shows the full log grouped by ship day with a running count (19 improvements landed on Aug 25 alone), a momentum line derived from the log itself, and a 'See it live' link on every entry — the log names where in the app each change lives, so the page doubles as a guided tour. The covered-markets band now runs here too, same as /why and /demo.

entries.title: The sample screen says where Philadelphia sits in the pack
entries.blurb: The demo's asset-type line now carries pack positions from the same shared ranking builder as the market page: Philadelphia office #10 of 18, industrial #17 of 17 — the wide 10.3–15.5% two-tracker band honestly lands it loosest — and multifamily #6 of 18. Retail carries no rank because its numeric level is held open, so no position is invented. Ranks run tightest first, and all three surfaces (sample screen, metro briefs, rankings) derive from one function.

entries.title: The cap hunt continues — two more templated catches, real Yardi texture for Baltimore
entries.blurb: The Baltimore and Richmond multifamily cap fields stay honestly null after another sweep: the loan-store '5.6% across all classes' boilerplate turned up twice more — once spliced into a digest under Berkadia's Q1 framing (the fingerprint phrase gave it away; eighth sighting), once printed at the state level for all of Virginia (one number claiming to price every market in a state is self-refuting; ninth). A separate unattributed 'averaging 8.5–9%' claim was rejected for naming no research house. What did survive the filter: Yardi Matrix's March 2026 Baltimore print — 94.8% occupancy for stabilized assets (construct declared, not comparable to the vacancy band), $1,744/mo average advertised asking, Q1 absorption 219 units against 260 delivered.

entries.title: Rank chips on every brief — each sector read says where it sits in the pack
entries.blurb: Every metro brief's asset-type rows now carry a rank chip — Northern Virginia industrial reads #1 of 17, DC office #13 of 18 — computed from the same shared leaderboard builder as the rankings table and the homepage lens, so the three surfaces can never disagree. Chips only appear where a numeric vacancy ranks; a metro whose level is held open gets no invented position. Each chip clicks through to the full cross-metro ranking.

entries.title: The sector lens — the board now names the tightest market per asset class
entries.blurb: Under the pulse board, four chips carry the tightest covered market on file for office, industrial, multifamily, and retail — today that's four different metros (Hampton Roads office, Northern Virginia industrial, New York multifamily, Boston retail), each with its vacancy band kept as a band and a count of how many markets are ranked. Every chip opens the full cross-metro ranking, and both surfaces derive from the same shared leaderboard builder, so the homepage can never drift from the market page.

entries.title: Sector leaderboards — every covered market ranked, one asset class at a time
entries.blurb: The market page's asset-class explorer now flips the metro tiles the other way: pick office, industrial, multifamily, or retail and see every covered market with a numeric read ranked tightest to loosest — vacancy bands kept as bands (a spread is never averaged into one printed number), asking $/SF and cap ranges where sourced, a source link on every row. Metros whose level is honestly held open are named under the table, never silently dropped.
